subject: Tenant slice proxy placement & control/data demarc validation
messages:
From: Aarti Shah <aarti.shah@blueharbor.com>
To: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.com>
Cc: BlueHarbor Networking Team <netops@blueharbor.com>
Date: Mon, 12 Jun 2023 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Tenant slice: proxy placement question and MTLS boundary

Hi Mateo —

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. As we start mapping the tenant-slice for our on-prem pilot, we hit a couple of questions that affect control-plane reachability and whether the tenant proxy should sit in the customer pod vs. the edge DMZ. Short list: 

- If the proxy is inside the tenant pod (with host route to Redwood edge), how do we avoid hairpin NAT when control-plane callbacks go via the egress gateway?
- For mTLS: BlueHarbor will terminate TLS at our F5. Can Redwood’s control plane authenticate the runtime using a customer-supplied client cert chain (we need mutual auth to be visible in our audit logs)?
- Firewall: any ephemeral outbound ports or long-lived TCP flows we should reserve on our perimeter policy?

Can you point us at a minimal runbook and a diagram that shows the control-plane/data-plane demarc and recommended SNAT approach? We’d like to include this in our architecture review with security on Thursday.

Aarti
Network Architect | BlueHarbor Inc.
[attachment: example_f5_policy.txt (txt)]

From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.com>
To: Aarti Shah <aarti.shah@blueharbor.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 12 Jun 2023 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant slice: proxy placement question and MTLS boundary

Hi Aarti — thank you, good questions. I’ve attached a short runbook and a topology sketch that addresses the hairpin/SNAT and mTLS flow. High level answers first: 

1) Proxy placement and hairpin: we strongly recommend placing the Redwood tenant sidecar proxy in the tenant pod (closest to runtime). This minimizes cross-pod latency and keeps KV cache locality. To avoid hairpin when control-plane callbacks egress via your border:
   - Use asymmetric routing: advertise a host route from the tenant pod to the edge gateway via BGP/route-reflectors so return traffic to runtime goes directly to the pod IP (no SNAT).
   - If asymmetric routing is not possible, configure SNAT at the egress gateway with a consistent source IP (customer-provided NAT pool) and add DNAT rules at the edge to map control-plane replies back to the pod. We include both patterns in the runbook.

2) Mutual TLS: Redwood supports customer-provided client cert authentication for control-plane connections. We can configure our agent to present the client certs that you upload to the keystore (we'll accept PEM chain + private key via secure upload). We also log peer DN and cert fingerprint in control-plane audit events so your security team can ingest them.

3) Firewall ports: minimal set below — these are in the runbook as well:
   - Control-plane HTTPS: outbound TCP 443 from runtime to control-plane endpoints (we recommend allowing 443 to the Redwood edge IPs).
   - Long-lived streaming: websocket/tcp keepalive on 443.
   - Metrics/telemetry (optional): outbound 9411 (Zipkin-style) or 8080 for pull metrics if you run our sidecar push.

I’ve included an action checklist for Thursday’s review and attached: redwood_onprem_runbook_v1.pdf, tenant-slice-proxy-diagram.png, controlplane-dataflow-table.xlsx. Marissa — can you call out any operational guardrails we should highlight for the review? Jonas — any specific BGP/route cheat-sheets we should include?

Thanks,
Mateo
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
[attachment: redwood_onprem_runbook_v1.pdf (pdf)]

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 13 Jun 2023 08:21:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant slice: proxy placement question and MTLS boundary

+1 on the recommendations. A couple of ops notes to surface for the customer review: 

- Observability: if you choose consistent SNAT, add an HTTP header passthrough (X-Redwood-Tenant) so logs correlate to tenant ids — we can enable this in the proxy.
- Rollback: if you put the proxy in the pod and later need to shift to edge placement, we’ve seen 3 failure modes — DNAT mapping drift, certificate mismatch states, and DNS propagation lag. Add these to the cutover playbook (see runbook section 4).
- Capacity: edge-proxy placement centralizes burst handling. Call out the load-testing numbers we ran (see table on page 3).

I’ll draft the short slide (ops risks + mitigations) and drop a link in the review doc.

Marissa
Director, Private Deployments | Redwood Inference
[attachment: tenant-slice-proxy-diagram.png (png)]

From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
To: Aarti Shah <aarti.shah@blueharbor.com>, Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 14 Jun 2023 10:45:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant slice: proxy placement question and MTLS boundary

Aarti — a couple of practical BGP/route items to consider for Thursday: 

- Preferred: advertise host routes for your tenant IP range from the rack switch to the RedEdge router (no NAT required). We’ll provide a short prefix-list for the workshop.
- Fallback: if your infra team cannot advertise host routes, plan for a persistent SNAT pool and ensure the firewall policy maps the SNAT IP to the specific tenant slice service port ranges (avoid port collisions).
- Healthchecks: require a /healthz probe accessible from your edge router (TCP 443) to avoid blackholing flows during failovers.

I added a short BGP cheat-sheet to the Drive link.

Jonas
Staff Network Engineer | Redwood Inference
